Polls (E6): hydration reads each live message's poll and its votes in one batch per page and counts them, naming voters on each choice only when the poll is not anonymous. createPoll, pollRules, pollChoices, setPollChoices (which says whether anything changed), closePoll and anonymousPollChoices (for the snapshot, those the account can still read) serve the routes; deleteMessage deletes the poll and redactEventRows drops poll from the log's copies.

listSharedFiles (E7) lists the files on live messages one account can read, by the download rule (public, or a member and no guest), newest first by message id and then file id, and narrowed by kind (from FILE_TYPE_MATCH, so search and the browser agree; a picture is never a document), sharer, conversation and every word of q in the name, LIKE wildcards escaped. CROSS JOIN keeps files the outer loop, walking idx_files_message so a page stops once it is full; a test checks the plan.

Sidebar sections (E8): ChannelPrefs carries sectionId from channel_members.section_id. setChannelPrefs keeps a conversation in one place: a section clears its star and a star clears its section. sidebarSections lists an account's in order; createSidebarSection adds one last; renameSidebarSection, deleteSidebarSection (clearing its members' section_id and saying which) and orderSidebarSections (only the exact set) act on the account's own only.

Profiles (E9): a user row gives timeZone, away and avatarVersion only when set, so older comparisons of users still hold. updateUser sets the first two; isAway, avatar and setAvatar keep the rest, setAvatar with null deleting the bytes.
A message row's call_kind becomes Message.call, and createMessage keeps one (E10).

Two-step sign-in (E11): twoStep reads an account's key, last step and recovery codes left; twoStepUserIds lists who has it. enableTwoStep, disableTwoStep (which says whether it was on) and replaceRecoveryCodes are called inside a transaction; useTwoStepStep keeps the step a code was accepted for, and useRecoveryCode spends a code once.

Blocks and reports (E12): blockedIds and setBlocked; reports are kept by admin/reportStore.ts. NOT_BLOCKED leaves a blocked author out of unreadMentionCounts and activityMessages; listFriends leaves out a request from someone blocked.

entries.plain: Names the server's version and the exact code it was built from, for backups and network announcements.
entries.summary: Names the server version and exposes source identity stamped into builds.
details: A small standalone module avoids loading HTTP, sockets and discovery just to label a backup or announcement.
Built output includes revision and dirty state; source execution reports no build stamp rather than inventing one.
Version describes the release interface while revision/dirty identifies the actual source behind an artifact.

entries.plain: Tells browsers how long to keep saved copies of the web version's files, so pages load fast and updates arrive cleanly.
entries.summary: Applies cache rules that keep static delivery fast and upgrades coherent.
details: Content-hashed assets receive a one-year immutable cache lifetime because changing content produces a different filename.
HTML and other stable names use no-cache so a browser revalidates the page that points to the current asset hashes.
A missing /assets/ request returns a genuine asset miss rather than the single-page application's HTML; an obsolete JavaScript chunk should not be delivered as HTML.

entries.plain: The shared rules for finding a workspace on the local network and for building invite links that open in OwnBase.
entries.summary: Shares LAN discovery and invitation-link addressing conventions.
details: Defines the mDNS service type, default port and TXT fields including the per-start instance ID used by health verification.
The icon TXT field names the workspace icon's version; isIconVersion takes it only in the form a server makes (16 hex digits), since anyone on the network can announce anything.
hostWithPort brackets IPv6 literals correctly; isLinkableAddress excludes zone-specific and link-local addresses that ordinary browser URLs cannot use.
ownbase:// is the one deep-link scheme the desktop app registers and reads.

entries.plain: The shared description of what the desktop app tells its screens about hosting, backups, relays, screens and microphones.
entries.summary: Data types and error codes the desktop bridge carries, declared once for main and UI.
details: In protocol because it changes least: the UI's Platform and the desktop app's bridge contract both import it, and neither imports the other.
DesktopErrorCode lists the failures the UI acts on (quitting, the registry's three formats, a missing owner account, each relay field); anything else is failed with a message written to be shown.
isPort, portFromText and PORT_RULE are the one port rule (1 to 65535) the host dialog and the hosting controller share.

entries.plain: The one list of events an outside app can subscribe to, and what it must be allowed to read for each.
entries.summary: APP_EVENTS: each app event type with the scope it needs per kind of conversation; APP_EVENT_TYPES, appEventType, isAppEventType, eventScope and eventScopes read it (untangle U3).
details: The server's delivery, the subscription request schema (a subscription naming any other type is refused) and the Apps dialog's picker and missing-scope warning all read this list; the server's event registry must give each type a Slack shape and an actor.

Message events need the history scope of their conversation's kind; reactions, pins and users their own read scopes; channel and membership events channels:read or groups:read. A workspace-wide event reads as public.

entries.plain: The one rule for when a typed message is a slash command, and the list of commands the app runs itself.
entries.summary: parseCommand reads `/name args`; COMMAND_NAME is the stored name rule; IN_APP_COMMANDS lists /poll, /away, /status and the rest with their hint and whether they need a channel (untangle round 1).
details: The server lists and reserves the in-app names but refuses to run them; client-core's send hands one back to the caller instead of sending it, and the Composer runs it.
The space or end after the name keeps a pasted path such as /Users/me/notes.txt an ordinary message.

entries.plain: The shared rules for what a person, channel, message, file and every other workspace record looks like.
entries.summary: Defines the shared vocabulary of workspace records and feature metadata.
details: Models users/roles, room types, memberships, messages, files, actions, invitations, audits, sessions, schedules, apps and forms without coupling the server to React or browser DOM objects.

Message seq identifies its creation event; a live payload can have seq 0 until the client applies the envelope's sequence. Thread replies and channel-broadcast replies remain the same underlying message.
Follow records include revision and unread-hold state; operational status models storage, queues, retention, connections and event-loop delay.
Optional capability/metadata fields allow older servers and clients to interoperate without assuming support.
The shared 30-day send retry window aligns client automatic retries with server retention of minimal send keys after content is removed.
Role includes guest, and ServerInfo.accessPolicy says who may join; an older server omits it, which clients read as accounts only.
APP_SCOPES (Slack's names) and DEFAULT_APP_SCOPES (posting only) (E18c); which events an app can be sent, and with which scope, is appEvents.ts.
ChannelPrefs.starred is one account's star on a conversation (UX-20). Servers before schema 40 leave it out, which reads as unstarred.
AuditAction includes workspace.renamed and workspace.access_policy_changed, with the target type workspace, recorded with the old and new value.
ServerInfo.iconVersion gives the icon's version, or null, before sign-in; it is absent from older servers. The audit action workspace.icon_changed records a set or a removal (UX-60).

Message.forwardedFrom is a ForwardReference: the original's id and conversation, and its author, words, files and time unless it is hidden (a private original forwarded elsewhere) or deleted. Servers before forwarding leave it out (E1).

Message.previews is LinkPreview[] (E2): id, the address as written, title, description, siteName, and the picture's size or null. Absent when a message has none and from older servers. AuditAction includes workspace.link_previews_changed.
ThreadFollow.muted is true for a thread this account muted and absent otherwise, and from servers before schema 43 (E3).
Reminder is one account's reminder about one message: its conversation and thread, remindAt, and dueAt or null while it waits. ReminderItem pairs one with its message for the list (E4).

Message.poll is a Poll (E6): options, each with its text, votes and, unless anonymous, voterIds; multiple, anonymous, voters (how many people chose anything) and closedAt. An option is known by its place. POLL_OPTIONS_MIN and POLL_OPTIONS_MAX (2 and 10), POLL_QUESTION_MAX (300) and POLL_OPTION_MAX (80) are the rules both sides share.
SharedFile is one file as the file browser lists it (E7): its FileMeta, and the message that shared it, with its conversation, thread, sharer and time.

SidebarSection is one account's named sidebar section (E8); ChannelPrefs.sectionId is the one a conversation is kept in, or null. SIDEBAR_SECTIONS_MAX (50) and SIDEBAR_SECTION_NAME_MAX (80) are the limits both sides share.
User.timeZone, User.away (set by hand) and User.avatarVersion are present only when set (E9); a picture is served under its version.
Message.call is a CallNotice, a note the server left about a call as from its caller (E10); kind missed is a huddle nobody answered.
AuditAction user.two_step_reset is an admin turning off someone's two-step sign-in (E11).

ReportReason (spam, harassment, inappropriate, other), REPORT_NOTE_MAX (500), ReportResolution (dismiss, remove, deactivate), MessageReport and ReportedMessage are what a report carries to admins (E12); AuditAction report.resolved records what was done.

entries.plain: Describes the updates the server sends, both the ones replayed after a reconnect and short-lived ones like typing.
entries.summary: Defines durable replay events and private/live socket messages.
details: WorkspaceEvent covers durable message, channel, membership and user changes; EventEnvelope adds monotonically increasing seq for reconnect replay.
history.removed names whole thread roots so clients can invalidate removed root/reply content and files even when history is evicted.

EphemeralEvent carries presence, typing, read/unread changes, private saves/preferences/follows, correlated huddle admission and one-user app replies/forms; these are never replayed as durable history.
ReadySnapshot describes current visible state and replayFrom, while synced marks completion. A null replay cursor replaces cached history; resync is the legacy fallback.
The distinction lets a lost ephemeral notice recover through a new snapshot without preserving private/transient UI messages forever.

Flags on ReadySnapshot (huddleReports, inlineReplies, forwards, scheduledEvents, activityThreads, threadMutes, stars, linkPreviews) say what this server does, so a client offers nothing an older server would refuse or quietly drop.
workspace.accessPolicy tells everyone signed in who may join now, and ReadySnapshot.workspaceSettings says the server takes Workspace settings' changes (UX-60). Older clients ignore the event.

ReadySnapshot.workspaceIcon advertises the workspace icon and iconVersion gives its version or null; the workspace.icon ephemeral event tells everyone signed in of a new version or a removal. Older clients ignore both (UX-60).

message.updated may say previewsOnly: only the message's link previews changed, which is not an edit (E2). The ephemeral workspace.linkPreviews tells everyone signed in that previews were turned on or off.

reminder tells an account's own devices that one of its reminders was set, moved or came due, with the message when it came due; reminder.removed that one is gone. ReadySnapshot.reminders lists them, and is absent from a server that keeps none (E4).

message.updated may say pollOnly: only the message's poll changed, by a vote or its closing, which is not an edit (E6). poll.choices tells an account's own devices what it now chose in a poll; ReadySnapshot.pollChoices holds those for anonymous polls, and is absent from a server without polls.
ReadySnapshot.sharedFiles says the server lists shared files (E7); an older one is offered no Files.
sidebar.sections tells an account's own devices its sections after any change; ReadySnapshot.sidebarSections lists them, absent from a server that keeps none (E8).
ReadySnapshot.profiles says the server keeps pictures, time zones and away (E9), and a client's idle message says whether its device is idle.
huddle.ring carries a HuddleRing as it now stands (E10); ReadySnapshot.huddleRings lists those an account is part of and says the server rings; huddle.decline says no to one.
blocks tells an account's own devices whom it blocked, and reports tells the owner and admins how many reported messages wait (E12); ReadySnapshot.blocked and openReports give both at connection.

entries.plain: The list of every reason the server can give for turning a request down, so the app can only check for reasons that exist.
entries.summary: ERROR_CODES and the ErrorCode type, used by the server's HttpError and the client's ApiError.
details: Every code a REST answer can carry is listed once, grouped by what it is about, along with the few a client makes up itself when no answer arrives (network_error, upload_timeout, http_error).
HttpError on the server and ApiError in client-core both take an ErrorCode, so a code renamed or retired on one side fails to compile where the other still expects it.
errorCodeOf reads a code off the wire and turns one this client does not know into http_error.
Incoming webhooks answer in Slack's words (invalid_webhook, not_in_channel, no_text, invalid_payload); those are listed too, since the Apps dialog's test post reads them.

entries.plain: The pieces every REST route is described with: who may call it, what it reads, what it answers and how long a client waits.
entries.summary: EndpointSpec, endpoint(), the Access levels, and the types that read a declaration's params, query, body and answer (untangle U2).
details: Access is public, guest, member, admin, owner or bot. whileLocked marks a route an account that must choose a new password may still reach; ticket marks one a one-time ?download= ticket can stand in for the session on.

A body is a zod schema, or image (the picture itself, typed by its Content-Type), file (a multipart upload) or slack (Slack's arguments, read by the route so its refusals keep Slack's shape). An answer is json<T>(), bytes, text or page.

endpoint() fills in DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS (10 s) when a declaration names no timeout. PathParams, QueryOf/QueryIn, BodyOf/BodyIn and AnswerOf give the server's handlers and the client's calls their types from one declaration.
fillPath encodes every path parameter, so an id or emoji holding /, ? or # stays one segment.

entries.plain: The list of every REST route the server answers, each written down once, which both the server and the apps read.
entries.summary: endpoints: each route's method, path, access, query and body schemas, answer type, success status and client timeout; extensionRoutes for routes at paths the server names (untangle U2).
details: The server registers each entry through route() and the client's Api calls each by its name, so a path, a body or an answer changed here changes on both sides at once, and neither can name a route the other lacks.
Which routes guests reach and which an account with a temporary password reaches are read from the access levels here; there is no separate list to keep in step.
Slack's Web API methods (auth.test, chat.postMessage, views.*), the command response URL and incoming webhooks are declared too, with body slack, so they keep Slack's wire shapes.

extensionRoutes are the shapes of routes an extension offers at paths it names in ServerInfo or a settings panel (P9): ee declares them at its own paths, and the client calls them at the path it was given.
packages/server/openapi.json is built from this table by the server's openapi test.

entries.plain: Shared formatting rules for showing text exactly as typed and spotting @channel, @here and @everyone mentions.
entries.summary: Shares literal mrkdwn escaping and room-wide mention interpretation.
details: escapeMrkdwn prefixes formatting delimiters and backslashes so generated text such as /shrug is displayed literally.
broadcastsIn recognizes Slack-compatible <!channel>, <!here> and <!everyone> tokens, normalizing everyone to channel.
broadcastLabel turns wire tokens into user-facing labels; choosing who is eligible for notification remains an authorization/presence decision elsewhere.
USER_MENTION and userMentionsIn read <@id> mentions; the server's mention index, its mention-count fan-out, notifications and the UI all use them instead of their own patterns.

entries.plain: The shared rules for the messages that set up a huddle, including which side starts the call so both do not at once.
entries.summary: Describes peer-call signaling and deterministic offer ownership.
details: Offer, answer, ICE and explicit camera/screen/muted/screenSound messages are plain serializable objects usable by both server and browser. They are zod schemas (huddleSignal, callReport) with the types derived from them, so the socket schema and the types cannot differ.

screenSound is said, true or false, only by a client with a fourth slot for a share's sound, and tells the other side it may send there. A client from before that slot never says it, and is sent nothing on it, since it would take any fourth track for the person's microphone.

view, in a media signal, says how tall its sender draws the camera and the share of the one it goes to, rounded to a few heights, and 0 for not drawn (E13b); that side then sends no bigger, or nothing. A server from before it strips the field, and the call is sized by its size alone.
Explicit media flags distinguish an active camera from a silent negotiated slot; a receiver track's muted flag alone is not evidence that frames exist.
shouldInitiateOffer uses user-ID ordering so two peers discovering each other do not both offer simultaneously.
HuddleState lists live participants. The protocol carries handshake/control state rather than audio or video bytes.
CallReport, CallCause, CandidateKind and CallLogEntry describe what a side saw of a connection and the server's call log, without addresses or SDP.
HuddleRing is a direct message's huddle ringing the people in it (E10): its caller, when it started and runs out, and who it still rings, who answered by joining and who declined.

entries.plain: Gathers all the shared rules in one place so the app and the server use exactly the same ones.
entries.summary: Exports the common protocol modules through one package entry.
details: Re-exports entity, event, REST validation, discovery, search, formatting, huddle and permission contracts.
Server, client and UI consume the same names instead of copying request shapes or subtly different policies.
Runtime helper/schema imports can affect bundling, so constants needed by lightweight consumers are kept outside schema-heavy definitions where practical.

entries.plain: Decides who can manage a channel, such as adding or removing people, with the same rules in the app and on the server.
entries.summary: Shares channel-management policy between server enforcement and UI affordances.
details: isAdministrator is the one owner-or-admin check, used by the server, the gateway and the UI.
Owner/admin, creator and delegated member managers receive different management powers; active human status and room type are checked.
Delegated management ends with membership. Removing someone is not a public-room ban, and an administrator's management role does not grant visibility into private rooms.
Removal protects self, owner, admins and privileged managers according to the actor's authority; manager assignment rejects inappropriate bot/deactivated/creator targets.
Visibility must be checked separately by the server even when a management helper returns true.

entries.plain: Says how many members a workspace's plan includes, and counts the members, the same way on the server and in the app.
entries.summary: The MemberNotice shape the server sends its owner and admins, and planMembers, the count it is compared with (P5).
details: MemberNotice carries the plan's member count and, when the host gave them, its name and an upgrade address; the ready snapshot holds it for the owner and admins only.
planMembers counts people who can sign in: apps, guests (who last a day) and deactivated accounts are left out.
It is a notice, never a limit: nothing on the server refuses a join or a sign-in because of it.

entries.plain: Lets parts that live outside the server, such as the Enterprise edition, plug into it without the server ever depending on them.
entries.summary: The ServerExtension point and the command line's extension registry (P6).
details: A ServerExtension registers routes after the server's own (with requireUser, requireAdmin, requireOwner and memberCount from the server), adds a line to the workspace status, gives the owner and admins a notice in their snapshot, and is stopped with the server.

A CommandLineExtension names its flags and help; main.ts merges them into parseArgs and --help and makes the extension from them, so a setting it cannot use is refused with a ConfigError like the server's own.
The MIT code never imports an extension: a build's entry (ee/src/main.ts) adds one with addCommandLineExtension before importing main.ts.

Signing in (P9): signInMethods() goes into server-info as signIn {methods, passwords}, requiresSingleSignOn() makes the login, register, guest-account and two-step routes refuse everyone but the owner with sso_required (asked only once the password is right), and settingsPanels() is what GET /api/admin/extension-settings shows the owner.

The context also gives storage (meta keys under extension:<name>:, listed by prefix with substr, not LIKE), users (get, byHandle, create a member nobody knows a password for, joined to the public channels), startSession and publicUrl.

entries.plain: Checks an Enterprise license on the server itself, offline, and says whether it is good, in its 14 days of grace, or over.
entries.summary: Reads OWNBASE-LICENSE-1 lines: Ed25519 signatures against trusted public keys, then the claims and where they stand in time.
details: A license is claims (id, licensee, plan, members, features, issuedAt, expiresAt) in base64url JSON, signed with Ed25519 over the prefix and claims; node:crypto alone checks it.
readLicense never throws: anything that is not a license, was changed, or was signed by a key the build does not trust is invalid with a reason in words.
An ended license is in grace for 14 days, features still on (featuresOn), then expired; one dated more than a day ahead of the server's clock is refused.

entries.plain: Names the environment variables a license is read from, so the hosting control plane passes the same ones on.
entries.summary: LICENSE_ENV: LICENSE_FILE and LICENSE, read as OWNBASE_<name> by the command-line extension.
details: Kept apart from enterprise.ts so ee/cloud can import the names without bundling the edition itself.

entries.plain: Lists the public keys whose licenses this build accepts. The private keys are kept elsewhere, never here.
entries.summary: TRUSTED_LICENSE_KEYS, base64url raw Ed25519 public keys, empty until the first key is made.
details: With no key listed no license is accepted, and the server runs as the free edition.
A key that has issued licenses stays listed while they run, so a new key can be added without breaking old licenses.

entries.plain: Puts the Enterprise edition in a running server: the license's state, what the owner and admins are told, and which features are on.
entries.summary: The enterprise ServerExtension and its --license command-line part.
details: enterprise() works out where the license stands each time it is asked, so one ending while the server runs ends on time; has(feature) is what Enterprise features will ask.
It adds GET /api/admin/license for the owner and admins, a workspace status line, and one notice at a time: ended, in grace, ending within 30 days, or more members than it covers.
enterpriseCommandLine reads --license, OWNBASE_LICENSE_FILE or OWNBASE_LICENSE; a license that is not one stops the server at the door, an ended one does not.
It carries single sign-on (sso.ts), on while the license has the sso feature: its routes, sign-in methods, the require-SSO rule and the owner's panel.

entries.plain: The Enterprise edition's own routes, written down the same way as the server's.
entries.summary: eeEndpoints: the license route and the single sign-on routes, registered through the server's route(); ssoSettingsBody (P6, P9, untangle U2).
details: The single sign-on routes the client reaches at a path the server names take their shape from extensionRoutes, so the client's call and ee's route cannot disagree.
POST /api/sso/connect is declared guest, so a guest who asks reaches its own check and is told guests sign in with their name alone, rather than the server's general refusal.

entries.plain: Talks to a company's sign-in service the OpenID Connect way, and checks that what it sends back is really from it, for this workspace, and still current.
entries.summary: A small OpenID Connect client: discovery, PKCE, token exchange, ID token checks (P9).
details: discover() reads <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration, wants the issuer it names to be the one asked for, and https everywhere except loopback, where tests and local providers run; it picks client_secret_basic unless only client_secret_post is offered.
authorizationUrl() asks for openid email profile with state, nonce and an S256 code challenge; exchangeCode() posts the code and verifier and wants an id_token back.

verifyIdToken() checks the signature with node:crypto against the provider's published keys (RS, PS and ES algorithms, never none or HS), then iss, aud and azp, exp and iat with a minute of clock skew, the nonce and sub. KeySet reads the keys when first needed and again, at most once a minute, for a key id not seen before.

entries.plain: Single sign-on for the Enterprise edition: the owner sets it up, people link their company account or get one, and the sign-in screen gets its button.
entries.summary: The single sign-on routes, links between accounts, and the owner's settings (P9).
details: GET /api/sso/start sends the browser to the provider with a state kept in memory for 10 minutes and bound to the browser by an HttpOnly cookie; a sign-in carries the client's challenge, a link to an account a one-time ticket from POST /api/sso/connect.

GET /api/sso/callback uses the state once, wants the same browser, checks the ID token, then links the account, finds the one linked, or makes one where the owner allows it (verified addresses at the domains given). It hands back a two-minute one-time code: <public>/#/sso/<code> in a browser, an ownbase://sso link on a page for the desktop app. POST /api/sso/redeem turns it into a session only with the verifier whose SHA-256 the start had.

Links are kept in the extension's storage as sso:identity:<hash of issuer and subject> and sso:user:<id>, so changing the issuer leaves old links unused. Accounts have no email, so nothing links by one.
Without the license feature, people already linked still sign in, but nothing new is set up, linked or made, and passwords come back. The settings never send the client secret.

entries.plain: Starts the server with the Enterprise edition in it; the server bundle is built from this file.
entries.summary: The command line's entry for builds with ee/: adds the Enterprise extension, then imports the server's main.ts.
details: The registry is filled before main.ts is evaluated, since main.ts reads it as it parses the flags.
Backups taken in a child process run this same file, which reaches the backup command before any license is read.

entries.plain: The front door of the Enterprise edition, for code that uses its license checks.
entries.summary: Re-exports enterprise, the license reader and the trusted keys.
details: Nothing outside ee/ imports it; ee/test/boundary.test.ts checks that.

entries.plain: Starts OwnBase's hosting: the control plane that runs a server for each hosted workspace and tells Caddy about them.
entries.summary: The ownbase-cloud command line, built into one file beside ownbase-server.js.
details: Reads --data, --domain, --listen, --server, --ports, --caddy-admin, --tls and --upgrade-url, and the operator's token from OWNBASE_CLOUD_TOKEN or OWNBASE_CLOUD_TOKEN_FILE (32 characters or more); a setting it cannot use stops it at the door.
Listens on loopback by default, starts every active workspace, and tells Caddy the whole config again every five minutes in case Caddy restarted without its last one.
On SIGINT or SIGTERM it stops each workspace's server itself before going.

entries.plain: Creates, pauses, restarts, copies and deletes hosted workspaces, and answers the operator's requests to do so.
entries.summary: ControlPlane: the registry, the supervisor and Caddy behind an operator API.
details: Each workspace runs ownbase-server on its own loopback port with --public-url https://<slug>.<domain>, --trust-proxy, its plan's --storage-limit-mb and --member-notice, daily backups, and OWNBASE_CLAIM_CODE; only the system's settings and the call relay's are passed on from the control plane's environment.
POST /api/workspaces answers with the owner's claim link, <url>/#/claim/<code>, until someone has claimed the workspace; a workspace that does not start is taken back out, folder and all.

Suspending stops the server and shows a paused page at the address; export stops it, runs backup and verify-backup into exports/, and starts it again; delete exports first, then removes the folder and keeps the address taken.
Changes go one at a time. GET /caddy/ask, which needs no token, says whether a name is a workspace's, so Caddy only gets certificates for those.

entries.plain: Keeps each hosted workspace's server running, and starts it again if it stops on its own.
entries.summary: Supervisor: one child process per workspace, restarts with growing waits.
details: start waits for /api/health to answer (30 s at most), and gives up as soon as the server is stopped instead.
A server that stops on its own is started again after 1, 2, 5, 10, 30 and then 60 seconds; one that ran for a minute starts the waits over. Its output and each stop go to the workspace's server.log.
stop asks with SIGTERM and kills after 10 seconds; a stopped server is never started again by a waiting timer.

entries.plain: Writes Caddy's configuration for the hosted workspaces, and hands it to Caddy.
entries.summary: caddyConfig and loadCaddyConfig: the whole config, through Caddy's admin API.
details: Each active workspace's address goes to its server on 127.0.0.1; a suspended one's answers 503 with a page saying it is paused; a deleted one is gone.
Certificates are issued on demand, with the http permission module asking the control plane's /caddy/ask; the issuer is ACME, or Caddy's internal one for a test machine.
The config is loaded whole with POST /load each time, so Caddy never drifts from the registry.

entries.plain: Remembers which workspaces are hosted, on which plan, port and address, and in what state.
entries.summary: Registry (node:sqlite), the plans, and the rules for a workspace's address.
details: Team includes 50 members and 25 GB, Business 200 members and 100 GB; the server is told both.
An address is 3 to 32 lowercase letters, digits and single hyphens, and not one OwnBase keeps for itself, such as www or admin.
A deleted workspace keeps its row, so its address never leads to someone else; its port is free again. Claim codes are 24 random bytes in base64url.

entries.plain: The control plane's parts, for its tests and for code that drives it.
entries.summary: Re-exports the control plane, registry, supervisor and Caddy config.
details: Nothing outside ee/ imports it; the MIT code knows nothing of hosting.

entries.plain: Checks the shape and size of everything the app sends the server, such as names, passwords, messages and scheduled sends.
entries.summary: Validates the shared HTTP request bodies and paging/search parameters.
details: Zod schemas bound handles, passwords, profile fields, channel types, message text/files, scheduling, integration URLs, form values, administrative updates and cursor formats.
Messages require words, attachments or a message they forward (forwardFrom); DM creation has a fixed counterpart count and group DMs have a bounded participant list.
Scheduling carries a stable nonce; editing a scheduled message carries expectedText so a conflicting edit can be refused.
Integration URLs reject embedded credentials and non-HTTP(S) schemes. Modal submissions bound nested IDs and values before echoing them to an app.
Types are inferred from the schemas, keeping compile-time client contracts aligned with the server's runtime parsing. Parsed shape alone does not imply authorization.
channelPrefsBody takes notifyLevel, muted and starred, each optional. An older server's schema drops starred without an error, which is why clients wait for ReadySnapshot.stars.

workspaceNameSchema is the one rule for a workspace's name, for its host and its admins: 1 to 80 characters once trimmed, no control characters. workspaceNameBody and accessPolicyBody are Workspace settings' requests (UX-60).
WORKSPACE_ICON_TYPES (PNG, JPEG, WebP; no SVG), WORKSPACE_ICON_MAX_BYTES (256 KB) and WORKSPACE_ICON_PIXELS (256) are the one rule the server and the client share for the workspace icon (UX-60).
linkPreviewsBody is Workspace settings' request to turn link previews on or off (E2).
threadMuteBody is the request to mute or unmute a thread (E3).
reminderBody is the time to be reminded at, in epoch ms (E4).

sendMessageBody.poll makes a message a poll (E6): two to ten different choices of up to 80 characters, multiple and anonymous defaulting to false, and a question of up to 300 characters. pollVotesBody is the choices a vote replaces the voter's with. SendMessageBody is the schema's input type, so a client may leave out what has a default.
sharedFilesQuery is the file browser's page (E7): limit (30, at most 100), a cursor of message and file ids, kind, userId, channelId and q.

channelPrefsBody takes sectionId (E8). sidebarSectionNameSchema is a section's name, 1 to 80 characters once trimmed and no control characters; sidebarSectionBody and sidebarSectionOrderBody are the requests to name one and to order them.

updateMeBody takes timeZone, an IANA zone kept under its current name, or null to forget it, and away (E9). PROFILE_PICTURE_TYPES, PROFILE_PICTURE_MAX_BYTES and PROFILE_PICTURE_PIXELS are the workspace icon's limits.

loginBody.twoStep says a client can answer a second step (E11). twoStepSignInBody takes the challenge and exactly one of code and recoveryCode; twoStepPasswordBody and twoStepCodeBody carry the account's own changes.
reportMessageBody and resolveReportBody carry a report and an admin's resolution (E12).

entries.plain: Understands search filters such as who sent it, where, and on which day, the same way in the app and on the server.
entries.summary: Parses search syntax and calendar-day filters identically on client and server.
details: Splits recognized from/in/has/type/before/after modifiers from free terms, records invalid calendar dates and normalizes handles/channel names.
Attachment categories map to MIME patterns and filename extensions for server SQL, letting UI hints describe the same filters the server applies.
before excludes the named day; after starts at the following day in the reader's IANA timezone. Day boundaries account for daylight-saving transitions instead of assuming 24 hours.
A bounded cache keeps at most 32 Intl.DateTimeFormat instances, avoiding repeated construction while preventing arbitrary timezone inputs from growing memory indefinitely.
This parser returns criteria; Store still adds current conversation visibility and safe query parameter handling.

FILE_KINDS and FILE_KIND_TYPES are the file browser's kinds (E7): image is type:image, document is type:pdf, document, spreadsheet and presentation, and other is the rest. isFileType tests one file against a type's own LIKE patterns and name endings, and fileKind sorts a file, a picture before a document, so the client names a kind as the server filters it.
currentZoneName gives the name the IANA database has now for the 19 zones Chromium, Electron and Node still give by an old one, such as Asia/Calcutta for Asia/Kolkata (E9).

entries.plain: Starts the server on its own and runs the host's backup, restore and account recovery commands.
entries.summary: runServerCli: parses flags, runs operator commands, or starts the standalone server.
details: Takes the build's command-line extensions as an argument, so an extension can never be registered after the command line has read its flags.
Parses flags/environment through the flag table, validates startup values, locates the built web client and chooses LAN or isolated loopback hosting.
Dispatches backup, verify-backup, restore and local account recovery commands before ordinary server startup.
Verification prints the consequences of starting a backup: app callbacks, queued messages, accepted sessions and host settings that must be configured again.
--name, --invite-only and --access-policy set up a new workspace only; on an owned workspace the start prints one line for each flag that disagrees (keptSettingsNotes).

entries.plain: The one list of every command-line setting, its environment variable and its help.
entries.summary: Declares each CLI flag once: type, default, OWNBASE_ environment fallback, --help lines and whether hosting may pass it.
details: parseArgs options, the options part of --help and the environment fallback are all derived from FLAGS.
ENV_SETTINGS lists settings given only by the environment; CLOUD_ENV is the subset OwnBase's hosting passes on from its own environment.
serverArgs builds a workspace server's arguments for ee/cloud, typed so only flags marked cloud can be passed.

entries.plain: What every part of the server is handed: the database, the live connections, the rules for checking requests.
entries.summary: ServerContext, the shared pieces each feature module is built on, and the shared access checks.
details: createWorkspaceServer builds one context and hands it to each feature; handlers are plain functions over it.
requireChannelAccess and requireVisibleMessage answer 404 for anything the caller may not read, without saying whether it exists.
rationWith turns the rate limiter into the 429 every feature throws.

entries.plain: Saves a change and its events together, then tells everyone who should hear about it.
entries.summary: recordEvent and mutate: one transaction per change, events published only after commit.
details: recordEvent appends to the event log, writes the event's declared effects and queues app deliveries inside the caller's transaction.
mutate commits, flushes the outbox's ahead-notices, runs after-commit effects, then publishes; a frame that cannot be sent resynchronizes every socket (REV-10).
onPublished lets the apps feature start a delivery round after events go out.

entries.plain: Runs the server's background jobs so one failing never brings the server down.
entries.summary: BackgroundWork: contained queue runs, after-commit work and housekeeping, with failures counted for admin status.
details: run() contains throws and rejections from timers and immediates (REV-01), counting failures per queue until it next succeeds.
afterCommitted logs work that fails after a commit instead of undoing the answer; maintain logs one housekeeping step without skipping the rest.

entries.plain: Catches a crash in one piece of work so the server keeps running.
entries.summary: contain(): runs work, hands a throw to a reporter, and reports whether it finished.
details: The one crash-containment wrapper: socket callbacks (gateway), outbox notices, background work and after-commit effects all use it.
A reporter that throws is swallowed too, so reporting cannot end the process.

entries.plain: Says once what each database table's rows look like, and checks every row read against it.
entries.summary: shape(): a table's columns (text, number, bytes, a fixed set of words, or NULL-able) typed once; get/all read checked rows.
details: Each feature store declares one shape per table and derives narrower or wider ones with pick() and with(), so no query casts its result.
oneOf()/oneOfOrNull() take an object keyed by every word of a protocol union, so a word added to the union and not to the column fails to compile.
A column missing from a query, NULL where it may not be, or of another type throws at that read instead of passing a wrong value on.

entries.plain: Knows when the server is stopping, and stops every timer and outgoing call when it does.
entries.summary: Lifecycle: closing flag, shutdown signal, interval timers, close and drain hooks.
details: Features register intervals and close hooks here; stop() closes them before waiting on anything, then aborts outbound calls.
laterTurn(work) gives a queue that took a full page its next page on a later turn (the attachment cleanup and the scheduled queue), asked for once however often, and dropped on close.
Drains (attachment removals, app event deliveries) run after the last request handler finishes and before the database closes.

entries.plain: One alarm clock for many things due at different times.
entries.summary: SoonestTimer: a single timeout armed for the soonest due row, re-armed after each round.
details: Used by reminders and status expiry; a time beyond setTimeout's range wakes the timer to wait again.
Cleared when the server starts stopping; never armed when off, as in an isolated copy.

entries.plain: Works out where a request came from and the address others use to reach this server.
entries.summary: Network: public URL, proxy trust, caller address, local-request check and request origin.
details: isLocalRequest refuses anything forwarded, anything to a server with a public URL, and any browser Origin that is not this server.
requestOrigin uses the configured public URL, forwarded headers only when a proxy is declared, otherwise the connection's own address.
setPublicUrl and setTrustLoopbackProxy let a desktop host change these while running.

entries.plain: Sets up the web server every request goes through, before any route is added.
entries.summary: createHttp: Fastify with request tracking, CORS, uploads, security headers, form bodies and the web client.
details: runningHandlers holds every handler still running so shutdown waits for them before closing the database.
Unknown Slack Web API methods answer unknown_method; the browser client is served with precompressed files and a fallback to index.html.

entries.plain: The workspace's own settings, like its name and who may join, each written down once.
entries.summary: SETTINGS registry and Settings: each workspace setting's meta rows, parsing, fallback and writes in one place.
details: workspaceId, workspaceName, accessPolicy (kept in step with the older invite_only row), linkPreviews, claimCode and the icon's three rows.

Store.settings reads and writes these meta rows for a running server, and stoppedWorkspace.ts through the same declarations for a stopped one; extensions get their own prefixed storage from extensionStorage().

entries.plain: Reads a stopped workspace's name, identity and icon straight from its folder, and renames it, without starting it.
entries.summary: Read-only readers plus a held rename for a workspace no server has open; it passes on workspaceFile.ts's file name for the desktop app.
details: readStoppedWorkspace, readStoppedIcon and readStoppedIconVersion open the database read only and read through Settings, so nothing is started, upgraded or changed; a missing or unreadable database reads as null.

renameStoppedWorkspace refuses a folder with no database (opening it would make an empty one), holds the workspace so a server started by hand cannot write the old name back, and gives a backup reading the file two seconds before failing.
The desktop app reads these through the @ownbase/server/stoppedWorkspace subpath, for Manage hosting's list, icons, renames and backup checks.

entries.plain: Names the file a workspace's data is kept in, and reads and writes its settings rows directly.
entries.summary: WORKSPACE_DATABASE, workspaceDatabase(dataDir), the workspace-name row and metaRows over a bare DatabaseSync.
details: WORKSPACE_DATABASE names workspace.db for the server, recovery, backups and the desktop app's list of hosted workspaces.
It imports nothing but Node, so a backup job reads the workspace's name for its manifest without loading the server (backupImports.test.ts checks the graph).
WORKSPACE_NAME_ROW is the row SETTINGS.workspaceName keeps the name in.

entries.plain: Lets people set a reminder on a message and tells them when it is due.
entries.summary: Reminder routes, the due-reminder timer and the reminders part of the startup snapshot.
details: Set, cancel and list; at most REMINDER_LIMITS.perAccount per account, at most five years ahead.
One SoonestTimer brings reminders due, dropping those whose message is gone or no longer readable, or whose account is deactivated; never in an isolated copy.

entries.plain: Saves reminders and finds the ones that are due.
entries.summary: ReminderStore: the reminders table's queries, its row type mapped once.
details: Reachable reminders are those whose message is still there and whose conversation the account can read.
Setting, removing and coming due each tell the account's devices through the outbox.

entries.plain: Says who hears about a reminder changing.
entries.summary: The reminder and reminder.removed events, heard by the account's own devices.
details: Spread into the event registry beside every other feature's events.

entries.plain: Lets people vote in a poll and lets its author close it.
entries.summary: Poll vote and close routes, and the anonymous choices part of the startup snapshot.
details: A vote replaces the account's choices; a closed poll, an archived channel or a choice outside the poll is refused.
Both change the poll's message with a message.updated marked pollOnly, which apps are not told of.

entries.plain: Saves polls and counts their votes.
entries.summary: PollStore: poll rules, choices, closing, and the polls of a page of messages with votes counted.
details: ofMessages counts votes for every poll among the messages being sent, in one query, for message hydration.
anonymousChoices is the account's own choices in anonymous polls, which nobody else is told.

entries.plain: Says who hears about a person's own poll choices.
entries.summary: poll.choices, heard only by the account's own devices.
details: Spread into the event registry beside every other feature's events.

entries.plain: Lets people pin messages for a whole channel, and save messages for themselves.
entries.summary: Pin, unpin, list pins, save, unsave and list saved routes, and the saved ids part of the startup snapshot.
details: Pinning needs the message to be readable; listing a channel's pins needs the channel to be.
Saved messages are an account's own: saving tells only its devices.

entries.plain: Saves pins and saved messages, and pages through them.
entries.summary: SavedStore: the pins and saved_messages tables' queries.
details: Lists page by cursor and leave out what the reader can no longer see.

entries.plain: Says who hears about pins and saved messages.
entries.summary: pin.added and pin.removed, heard by the channel's readers and sent to apps; saved, heard by the account's own devices.
details: Spread into the event registry beside every other feature's events.

entries.plain: Lets people schedule a message for later, and posts it when the time comes.
entries.summary: Scheduled message routes, the due-message loop and its hourly prune.
details: Scheduling goes through the posting rules (messages/posting.ts), so what sending would refuse later is refused now.
The loop posts a batch at a time, yielding between full batches; what the author can clear holds a row, what they cannot fails it, each with words for their list.
An isolated copy posts nothing; sent rows are kept a week as proof, then pruned.

entries.plain: Saves the queue of messages waiting to be posted.
entries.summary: ScheduledStore: the scheduled_messages queue's queries, with its row mapped once.
details: Rows are queued, held (with a time to look again), sent or failed; held rows wake early when what held them clears.
Each change tells the author's devices through the outbox.

entries.plain: Says who hears about a person's scheduled messages changing.
entries.summary: scheduled, heard by the author's own devices.
details: Spread into the event registry beside every other feature's events.

entries.plain: Shows a thread's replies, and lets people follow, mute and mark threads read or unread.
entries.summary: Thread history, follow, mute, read, unread and followed-threads routes, and the thread follows part of the startup snapshot.
details: Only a thread's root can be followed, muted or read; a root the caller cannot read is a 404.
Replying follows a thread automatically, in the message.created event's effects, so every way a reply is written does it.

entries.plain: Saves who follows each thread and how far they have read it.
entries.summary: ThreadStore: thread history, thread_follows rows, followers, unread counts and the Threads list.
details: A follow's revision orders its changes, so a device applies only the newest.
A reply seen in the channel counts as read in its thread too, unless the thread was marked unread since (READ_IN_CHANNEL).

entries.plain: Says who hears about a person following or reading a thread.
entries.summary: thread.follow, heard by the account's own devices.
details: Spread into the event registry beside every other feature's events.

entries.plain: The few database rules several features share, like what counts as unread or as a mention.
entries.summary: SQL fragments for unread, read-in-channel, mentions, blocked authors, guests and the channel timeline.
details: One definition each, so a badge count can never disagree with the list it opens.
The client's isMessageRead is the same rule as UNREAD.

entries.plain: Lets people search messages and see their mentions and reactions in Activity.
entries.summary: Search and Activity routes.
details: Search parses words and filters (from:, in:, dates in the caller's time zone) and refuses a query with nothing to look for.
Both page by cursor and only ever return messages the caller can read.

entries.plain: Finds messages by words, filters and mentions.
entries.summary: SearchStore: full-text search over messages and the Activity list's queries.
details: Few matches are read in full; many are searched within a recent window first (SEARCH_FEW_MATCHES, SEARCH_WINDOW), so a common word stays fast.
Activity reads mentions from message_mentions by the same rule as the badges (core/sqlRules.ts).

entries.plain: Gives calls the servers they connect through, keeps the call log, and leaves a note when a call is missed.
entries.summary: Builds the live huddles (rooms.ts) with the missed-call note they leave, and huddles' HTTP side: ICE/TURN configuration and the call log.
details: rtcConfig gives the host's STUN/TURN servers plus a relay password for this member, never the relay's API token or shared secret.
The host can replace the ICE servers or the relay while running; a refused relay leaves the old one.
A ring nobody answered posts 'Missed huddle' as the caller, through the posting rules, so someone who can no longer post there leaves none.

entries.plain: Lets people upload and download attachments, and removes the files nobody needs any more.
entries.summary: Upload, download, download-ticket, shared-files and storage routes, the blob removal queue and its timers.
details: Uploads stream to disk under the storage budget; a picture's size is read from its header.
A download ticket is issued through the router (ticketFor) for the file's path; a ticketed download is an attachment, and access is checked again after the disk is read.
Blob removals go a page at a time and wait while a backup copies attachments (holdingRemovals); orphaned blobs are queued at startup and abandoned uploads are freed hourly.

entries.plain: Saves attachments' details and the list of files waiting to be removed.
entries.summary: FileStore: files rows, shared files and the file deletion queue with its retry ladder.
details: A file waiting for a scheduled message is never counted as abandoned.
A deletion that fails waits longer each time (DELETION_RETRY_MS); an id the server never gives is set aside for good.

entries.plain: Lets people read, send, edit, delete and react to messages, adds link previews, and discards old history when retention is on.
entries.summary: Message routes and reactions, the link preview queue, the posting rules' setup, message removal and the retention sweep.
details: Every post goes through posting.ts; updateMessage and removeMessage are what apps and moderation use to change a message.
Link previews are fetched after commit by two workers with a small cache; never in an isolated copy or with previews turned off.
Retention removes whole threads past the window a pass at a time, each pass its own transaction, and logs one history.removed per conversation.
Removed messages' send keys are pruned hourly once no app could retry them.

entries.plain: Saves messages, their previews and reactions, and reads them back with everything they show.
entries.summary: MessageStore: creating, editing, deleting and listing messages, send keys, link previews, reactions, retention purges and hydration.
details: hydrate turns rows into whole messages in a few queries per page: files, reactions, previews, polls, replies and forwards.
Editing or deleting re-quotes and redacts the event log's copies through the store core.

entries.plain: Lets people make, join, leave and manage channels and DMs, set how each one notifies them, and organise their sidebar.
entries.summary: Channel, membership, read place, prefs, notify default, unread summary, sidebar section and removal-note routes, and the conversations part of the startup snapshot.
details: Who may invite, remove or make managers follows protocol's channelPermissions; guests stay in public channels.
joinPublicChannels puts a new account in every open public channel, as a new public channel takes in everyone.
The snapshot slice holds the visible conversations, memberships, last seqs, mention counts, removal notes, sidebar sections and the notify default.

entries.plain: Saves conversations, who is in them and how far each person has read.
entries.summary: ChannelStore: channels and DMs, membership, prefs, read cursors, sidebar sections, removal notes and unread mention counts.
details: Reading a channel reads the replies it showed too, unless the thread was marked unread since (UNREAD in core/sqlRules.ts).
Mention counts are read from message_mentions, so a badge costs what the account's mentions cost.

entries.plain: Lets people change their profile and status, set a picture, see who is in the workspace, add friends, block someone and report a message.
entries.summary: Profile, status, avatar, member list, friend, block and report routes; the status-expiry timer; the people part of the startup snapshot.
details: A status set to clear itself is cleared at its time by one SoonestTimer, for everyone to see, and on starting for those that ended while stopped.
Profile pictures meet the same checks as the workspace icon (checkedPicture in core/context.ts).
Guests cannot be friends; reports go to the owner and admins as an open-report count.

entries.plain: Saves accounts as others see them, their pictures, friendships and blocks.
entries.summary: PeopleStore: users rows mapped once (toUser), profiles, avatars, statuses, friends and blocks.
details: toUser is the one mapping from a users row to the protocol's User, shared with sessions in the store core.
mayInvite is the rule for who may invite, also read by invites.

entries.plain: Lets people join, sign in and out, set up two-step sign-in, change their password, manage their sessions, join as a guest and invite others.
entries.summary: Register, guest, login, second step, logout, password, two-step, session and invite routes, and the password-hashing slots.
details: Password derivations run two at a time at most (hashing); more is refused with auth_busy rather than queued.
Wrong guesses are rationed per address and per handle; a right password clears the handle's count.
The first account needs the claim code unless it comes from this machine; when an extension requires single sign-on, a password signs in the owner alone.
Guests join for a day, at most 200 at once, into public channels only.

entries.plain: Saves sign-ins, passwords, two-step keys and invites.
entries.summary: AccountStore: sessions, passwords, two-step secrets and recovery codes, guest sessions and invites.
details: Sessions are kept by token hash; a session unused for 30 days ends, a guest's after a day.
An invite's status reads its creator's standing now: a deactivated creator or one no longer allowed to invite disables it.

entries.plain: Plugs in the server's extensions, such as single sign-on, and gives them a way to make members and sign them in.
entries.summary: registerExtensions: hands each extension its routes, storage, member count, user lookup, member creation and session start.
details: An extension's storage is its own prefixed rows (Settings.extensionStorage), apart from the workspace's settings.

Members an extension makes have a password nobody knows, a username and name held to joining's rules, and join the public channels through accounts' makeMember as anyone joining does; none can be made while nobody owns the workspace.
Sessions start through accounts' startSession, the same step every sign-in takes.

flows.title: Signing in and catching up
flows.summary: Signing in with a password gives the app a sign-in key. The live connection then turns that key into an up-to-date view of the workspace, filling in missed updates only where it is safe.

steps.title: Check the request and limit guessing
steps.description: The server checks the sign-in form has the right shape. It limits wrong passwords per username and per network address, to slow down guessing. It believes what a middleman says about who is connecting only when the host turned that on and the middleman runs on the same computer.
steps.detail: REST schemas check the login body. Separate address and handle allowances bound guessing; proxy headers only count under explicit loopback trust.

steps.title: Check the password and start a session
steps.description: The server compares the password against a scrambled copy, never the password itself. If it matches, the server sends back a random sign-in key. It keeps only a scrambled copy of that key, with an expiry date and the account it belongs to.
steps.detail: scrypt verification checks the stored salt/hash. Only a random bearer token leaves the server; the session row stores its hash, expiry and account identity.

steps.title: Say hello before getting updates
steps.description: The app opens a live connection and says which version it speaks and the last update it saw. The server checks the sign-in is still valid and whether the account must change its password first. Only then does it load the whole workspace for this person and start sending live updates.
steps.detail: The socket schema validates protocol/version/cursor. Gateway checks the session and forced password-change state and reads the full snapshot before registering the connection.

steps.title: Fill in missed updates or start fresh
steps.description: If the app was away briefly, the server sends the updates it missed, leaving out channels the person can no longer see. If the app was away too long, or its place in the history is gone, the server tells it to replace its copy of the workspace. Either way, a final signal tells the app it is up to date.
steps.detail: Store filters replay to current public/member access. If the cursor is pruned, invalid or beyond the replay budget, ready requests replacement; otherwise missed events replay and synced finishes catch-up.

steps.title: Keep checking the sign-in
steps.description: The server checks the sign-in again as it sends updates and during regular check-ins. When a sign-in ends, the server cuts its connections. Who is online comes from who is connected right now, and is worked out again after a reconnect.
steps.detail: Delivery and heartbeats recheck sessions; revocation disconnects affected sockets. Ephemeral presence is derived from live socket groups and rebuilt at reconnect.

flows.detail: Authentication produces a session; the socket handshake turns it into visible current state plus any safe replay.

flows.title: Saving a message on the server
flows.summary: The server saves a message the same way whether someone sends it now or it was scheduled earlier. Saving and announcing happen in a fixed order, so what is saved and what everyone sees always agree.

steps.title: Check the message and its files
steps.description: The server checks the message is within size limits, the sender's account is active and they can post in this channel. The channel must not be archived, and a reply must point at a real thread. Attached files must belong to this person and channel, and not already be set aside for another scheduled message.
steps.detail: Parse bounded message input, check active account/current channel access, archived state and a valid root. Files must belong to this account/channel and cannot be promised to another schedule.

steps.title: Spot a repeated send
steps.description: Each send carries a one-time code chosen by the sender's device. If the same code comes again with the same content, the server returns the message it already saved instead of posting a second copy. If the content differs, or that message was since deleted or cleared away by old-history cleanup, the server refuses.
steps.detail: Hash the request shape under the account-scoped nonce. An identical retry returns its message; conflicting content or a key for deleted/retained history is refused rather than creating a second post.

steps.title: Save the message and its update together
steps.description: In one step, the server saves the message, links its files, records its code and writes the update that announces it. The same step records deliveries to outside apps that should hear about it. Either all of this is saved or none of it is.
steps.detail: Create and hydrate the message, attach files, record its request key and append message.created in one synchronous transaction. Eligible app delivery rows are queued with that event.

steps.title: Mark a scheduled message as sent
steps.description: For a scheduled message, the same step marks the schedule as sent, links it to the new message and clears the schedule's own copy of the words and file list. A crash cannot leave one half done without the other.
steps.detail: For a scheduled send, the same transaction marks the schedule sent, links the message and clears queue text/file IDs. A crash cannot commit only one side.

steps.title: Announce it after saving
steps.description: Only once everything is saved does the server send the update to people allowed to see it. It groups together the updates for people following the thread or mentioned in it. Deliveries to outside apps go out separately, with a limited number of retries.
steps.detail: Gateway fans out only committed events under current visibility. Targeted follow/mention updates are coalesced, while app deliveries run through the bounded retry pump.

flows.detail: The same posting path handles direct sends and due schedules so persistence and live publication agree.

flows.title: Pressing a button on an app's message
flows.summary: Short-lived permissions tie each button press and form to the right app and person, and to what they may see right now. Extra checks handle a form sent twice at once and replies that arrive late.

steps.title: Show only buttons OwnBase supports
steps.description: Apps lay out their messages the way Slack apps do. The server keeps only text, buttons that open a web link and buttons that tell the app they were pressed, all within size limits. The message a button sits on decides which app and conversation the press belongs to.
steps.detail: Block Kit text/actions become bounded native text and HTTP(S) link or callback buttons. The pressed message determines the owning bot and conversation.

steps.title: Give the app short-lived permission
steps.description: When someone presses a button, the server tells the app and hands it two short-lived permissions, one to open a form and a reply address to update the message. These expire, and only so many can exist at once. Every call to an app is signed, has a time limit and cannot reach private computers on the host's network.
steps.detail: The callback receives an app-bound trigger and a response URL. Capability maps cap memory and expire permissions; outbound calls are signed, deadline-bounded and private-host-checked.

steps.title: Open the form for the right person
steps.description: The app uses its permission once to open a form. The server first checks that the app, its bot, the person and the channel are all still allowed. It then sends the form, with only the kinds of fields OwnBase supports, to that person alone.
steps.detail: views.open and views.push consume one matching trigger after current app, bot, person and channel checks. Supported fields become a view.open ephemeral event, carrying the person's whole stack, for the owner alone. views.update needs no trigger and changes a view still open.

steps.title: Refuse a second submission at the same time
steps.description: When the person submits, the server checks the form is theirs, required answers are filled in and each answer is one the field offered: an option it listed, someone with an account, a conversation the person can open, a real date. Only one submission of a form can be on its way to the app at a time, and a second one meanwhile is refused. Once the first finishes, the person can correct their answers or try again.
steps.detail: The server verifies form ownership, then readAnswer checks each value against its field and shapes it as Slack's state.values. One modal ID may have one callback in flight; overlap receives 409 view_submitting, and finally releases exclusion for correction or deliberate retry.

steps.title: Ignore late changes to an old message
steps.description: The app may later ask to replace or delete the message whose button was pressed. The server does this only if the message still looks as it did when pressed, and ignores the request if it was changed or deleted since. Each successful update through the same reply address becomes the version the next one must match.
steps.detail: Before replace/delete, current text/edit/actions must match the pressed revision. A disappeared or changed origin is ignored; successful updates through the same response URL advance its own expected revision.

steps.title: Know what a retry can still repeat
steps.description: The server stops overlapping submissions and checks again that permission was not withdrawn. Still, an app may act on a submission and then lose the connection before answering. If the person tries again, the app should spot the repeat by the form's ID.
steps.detail: The server prevents overlap and rechecks revocation, but an endpoint may perform its business effect before a transport failure. An app should deduplicate a retried view_submission by view ID.

flows.detail: Short-lived capabilities tie actions to the right app/person and current access, while N08/N09 control overlapping and delayed replies.

flows.title: Deleting messages and clearing old history
flows.summary: Deleting a message or clearing old history removes its words, buttons and file links from every working copy the server keeps, not just the one you see. The order of past updates stays intact, and a delayed resend cannot bring a deleted message back.

steps.title: Choose what to remove
steps.description: Deleting a message clears its words and buttons and anything live tied to it. If the host set history to expire, cleanup picks a thread only once its newest reply is old enough, then removes the whole thread. Each cleanup round handles a limited amount.
steps.detail: Soft deletion clears one message's words/actions and associated live state. Retention chooses roots only when their newest reply is old enough and removes the whole thread within a bounded pass.

steps.title: Clean up everything in one step
steps.description: The server handles even a very large thread in one go. It removes message and file links, keeps a bare record of each send code, lines up files for deletion and blanks stored copies of updates and app deliveries. It saves all of this together.
steps.detail: A temporary ID table handles large threads without bind-count limits. Message/file references, minimal purged send keys, queued blob deletions and redacted event/delivery copies commit together.

steps.title: Keep the order without the old words
steps.description: The server keeps a numbered list of past updates so apps can catch up in order. Updates that are out of date because the message was deleted or changed stay in that list, but lose their words, file details and button labels and links. A database upgrade also cleans copies left by earlier versions, including scheduled messages already sent.
steps.detail: Superseded event rows stay in the ordered replay log but lose text, file metadata and button labels/values/URLs. Schema 37 repairs earlier deleted/superseded copies and sent schedules.

steps.title: Tell connected people what was removed
steps.description: Once saved, the server tells everyone allowed to see it that a message was deleted or that history was cleared. For a whole thread it names the thread, so each person's app drops its saved copies of the thread and its replies and stops any file transfers for them.
steps.detail: After commit, message.deleted or history.removed reaches authorized sockets. Whole-thread root IDs let clients invalidate evicted root/reply caches and pending attachment transfers.

steps.title: Delete the files, retrying when needed
steps.description: A background job deletes the files a few at a time, and counts storage space as freed only once a file is gone. It tries a failed file again after a wait and keeps the failure visible, while the other files go ahead.
steps.detail: The file pump deletes bounded pages and releases storage accounting only after success. Retry delay and rejected rows let healthy removals proceed while failures remain visible.

steps.title: Know what cleanup does not reach
steps.description: These steps clean the copies in the working database. They do not remove the content from older backups, securely wipe space the database freed on disk, or recall what was already sent to outside apps.
steps.detail: Active database copies are cleaned. Historical backups, freed storage blocks and payloads already delivered to external apps are not recalled or securely erased by these operations.

flows.detail: N06/N07 and earlier retention work remove redundant words, actions and file references while preserving replay order and retry safety.

flows.title: Backing up and restoring a workspace
flows.summary: A backup is built and checked in full before it counts as a backup. Restoring keeps the original workspace, but a known gap remains while the folders swap.

steps.title: Copy the database at one moment
steps.description: The server copies its database as it stands, including the most recent saves, and lists the uploaded files the backup needs. If a file is deleted while the backup runs, the backup fails. To be sure a backup is complete, take it while the server is stopped.
steps.detail: VACUUM INTO reads committed SQLite/WAL state; snapshot file inventory identifies required blobs. Missing concurrent-deleted blobs fail capture, so stopped-server capture is the way to guarantee completeness.

steps.title: Or let the server back itself up
steps.description: A host can ask the server to take a backup on a timer into a folder of dated copies, keeping the newest few. Each is the same checked backup. While one copies files, the server holds off removing deleted ones, so the copy is complete without stopping anything, and the copying happens in a separate process so chat does not wait.
steps.detail: --backup-dir/--backup-every-hours/--backup-keep run BackupSchedule; the CLI's runner is a child `backup` process. File deletion flushes return early while a scheduled copy runs, and resume after it. Status reports enabled, interval, keep, last success, failures and next time.

steps.title: And send each one somewhere else
steps.description: A host can also have every scheduled backup sent as one zip to a storage bucket elsewhere, such as Cloudflare R2, keeping the newest few there. If the server's disk is lost, the backups are not. A send that fails is tried again within the hour without taking a new backup.
steps.detail: --backup-offsite https://<host>/<bucket>[/<folder>] with OWNBASE_BACKUP_OFFSITE_ACCESS_KEY_ID/_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY/_REGION. SigV4 PUT or multipart, then ListObjectsV2 and DELETE past --backup-offsite-keep. Status adds offsite.lastSuccessAt and failures. The control plane gives each hosted workspace <url>/<slug>.

steps.title: Or download a copy as the owner
steps.description: The owner can ask for a copy from Workspace settings without reaching the server. It is a fresh backup, checked like any other, sent as one zip file through a link that works once. The same zip restores the workspace here or on the owner's own server.
steps.detail: POST /api/admin/copy (owner only, free-space check) runs takeBackup with removals held; GET polls; a ticket bound to session and copy id streams a stored ZIP/ZIP64 with exact Content-Length. restore and verify-backup accept the .zip via withBackupFolder.

steps.title: Check the backup before keeping it
steps.description: The copied database and files must match their recorded sizes and fingerprints, the expected layout and counts, and the database's own health check. Every file reference must be valid, with nothing listed twice and nothing pointing outside the backup. Only then does the server move the finished backup to its final place.
steps.detail: Staged database and files must match checksums/sizes, schema/counts, integrity and references, with no manifest duplicates or path escape. Only then is the complete capture renamed to its destination.

steps.title: See what a restored copy would do
steps.description: Without changing anything, the host can list which outside apps a restored copy would contact, which scheduled messages are waiting, which app calls never went out and which sign-ins still work. A separate isolated mode runs the copy without calling apps or sending scheduled messages, so it can be looked at safely.
steps.detail: Read-only inventory reports app destinations, queued schedules, undelivered callbacks and surviving sessions. Isolated mode blocks app calls and schedule delivery while inspecting a restored copy.

steps.title: Prepare the restore beside the original
steps.description: Restore refuses to start if a server is using the workspace. It copies the checked backup next to the workspace folder and checks the copy again. The old workspace moves to a set-aside folder so it can still be recovered.
steps.detail: Restore refuses an already held workspace, copies the verified backup beside the target and verifies staged bytes. The old workspace is moved to a superseded folder for recovery.

steps.title: No other server can slip in while folders swap
steps.description: Restore has to let go of the workspace folder for a moment to rename it, because Windows will not rename a folder with a file open inside it. It keeps a second claim beside the folder the whole time, so a server started in that moment is refused and makes no workspace of its own there. If the swap fails, the original goes back where it was.
steps.detail: Restore holds a sibling path lock from before staging until publication or rollback is complete, and releases the in-folder hold only for the renames. holdWorkspace takes the path lock before mkdir, so a concurrent start gets WorkspaceInUseError and the target stays absent until the staged copy is renamed in.

steps.title: Start the restored workspace as usual
steps.description: The next server to start takes sole hold of the restored workspace and upgrades its database if needed, keeping a copy from before the upgrade. The host applies settings that belong to the computer separately, such as the public address, how long history is kept and call connection settings.
steps.detail: A subsequent server opens with the exclusive writer hold and atomic migrations, taking pre-upgrade copies when needed. Local host settings such as public URL, retention and ICE configuration must be applied separately.

flows.detail: Backups are staged and validated before publication; restore preserves the original and holds the target's path through folder replacement.
